It's raining heavily today. Phone's went off during your seminar about a flood warning, and even the professors were starting to fret. People sort of forget the presentation being displayed and begin to worry about how they'll get home—the people who have to run across campus to the dormitories are fine enough, but those who drive or take the bus or carpool are in a bit more of a tizzy. By this time, class gets dismissed and everyone disperses. Not many people attended today since it was the weekend, but you're one of the few.

It was raining early this morning when you got here, so you've got your umbrella prepared already. Tucked inside your rucksack—it's a bit of a small one, but it gets the job done until you can run to the dorms. You can barely see twenty feet in front of you once you're outside on the sidewalk, trees whistling with the wind and air rumbling with thunder. It's dark out, a hazy sort of purple that growls and sparks. 

Lightning is a fascinating phenomenon. Water—near atomic levels of minutia—freeze and separate across the atmosphere. As ice and water are shifted with the updrafts and downdrafts of the raging storm, electrons are sheared off miles above freezing level. Negative and positive charges are generated, and the electric field begins to *charge*. The atmosphere is an insulator; an inhibitor. It takes a tremendous amount of build up—but when that threshold is met, is broken... Opposites attract.

The moment your eyes met Phoebe's, lightning occurred.

She's knelt down in front of you, two feet planted in the azaleas. Her coat is off and draped over something, and she's soaked to the bone. It'd be funny enough to laugh if she weren't staring at you like a deer in the headlights, hair plastered to her face.

You don't know her well; she is a rather popular senior at your university and always surrounded by people. You know *of* her, and that is the limit. You know she's friendly and a conversationalist, that she has a part-time job, and that she doesn't live at the dorms and instead an apartment complex nearby. You've seen her in passing helping professors or tutoring students on campus, and every Monday she's with the college's radio club reading out announcements. She's like the sun, always drawing others in. Radiant.

Even now, she still shines brightly enough to blind you. 

"H-Hey, can you help me?" She asks, voice quaking and barely audible over the howling wind. "It's, uh, um... There's kittens. Can you help me get all of them?"

Phoebe's ears are burning.

They’re a bit of a novelty thing that don’t seen real; a bunch of singles meeting up to share drinks and maybe have fun together. Get to know each other, and all of that important *stuff*. You remember the time you took a cruise for a trip once when you were a little kid, and looking through the itinerary to see a mixer catered towards those forty and up. That sort of thing.

It was like a strange fantasy. Something that might happen in real life if the conditions were met, but were never exactly made or catered to you.

But, when a mutual friend of yours—a dumb, cocky meathead financial bro type—invited you and a plus one out for drinks with another group, you felt that this very well might be considered a mixer.

For all intents and purposes, the guy who invited you appears to be lying. There is no other group, and it’s just four of you—all people you know directly—sitting together splitting an appetizer from the bar and chasing it with some pretension craft beer. It’s boring.
